study.title: Biacuplasty has the strongest signal here
study.evidence_note: Narrative review summary; not a de novo systematic review.
study.confidence_note: Main figures are clearly stated, but this is a review article summarising older trials.
study.impact_line: Biacuplasty looks promising for selected refractory discogenic low back pain, but the evidence base is still dated and narrow.
summary: Three RCTs are summarised for biacuplasty, with better short-term pain and disability than control.
One trial compared with sham; another with conservative management; follow-up was mainly 6 months.
The review still calls for more RCTs and longer follow-up, especially on safety.

pico.p: Adults with chronic discogenic low back pain

limits: Review article, not a primary study.
Follow-up mostly short to mid term.
Some trials excluded obesity and smoking.
study.bottom_line: For selected patients with chronic discogenic low back pain, biacuplasty has the best-looking interventional evidence in this review. The evidence is still limited, dated, and not enough to treat it as routine care.

methods.design: Narrative review with updated literature search
methods.participants: Adults with chronic discogenic low back pain in the cited studies

results.result: Biacuplasty beat sham; NRS change 2.19 vs 0.6
results.detail: The review reports significantly larger pain reduction with biacuplasty than sham at 6 months.
The review reports significantly larger disability improvement with biacuplasty than sham at 6 months.

results.result: Biacuplasty + CMM beat CMM; VAS change 2.4 vs 0.56
results.detail: Compared with conventional medical management alone, the review reports significantly larger pain reduction with added biacuplasty.
The review reports more pain responders with biacuplasty plus conventional care than with conventional care alone.

how_to_apply: Consider only for refractory, well-selected discogenic cases.
Expect benefit estimates to be based on small, dated trials.
Do not oversell long-term durability or safety.
Use shared decision-making because evidence remains incomplete.
applies_to: Selected refractory chronic discogenic low back pain
Patients similar to the RCT populations
not_for: Cases where the diagnosis is uncertain

strengths: Summarises several RCTs for the same intervention.
Gives both pain and disability results.
weaknesses: Narrative review, not a systematic review.
No pooled estimate from this article.
Some cited studies excluded obese people and smokers.
appraisal.funding_conflicts: Authors report conflicts for two editorial board members; no trial funding for the summarised RCTs is provided here.

domains.reason: The article focuses on CDLBP interventions and the summary matches that aim.
A search was done, but the methods are not exhaustive or fully reproducible.
domains.support: P21: updated search and reference-list checking

domains.reason: The review reports trial findings but does not present a formal critical appraisal framework.
Findings are narratively summarised; no formal pooled analysis is presented in this article.

grade.reason: The review describes three high-quality RCTs for biacuplasty, including sham-controlled comparisons.
All three RCTs summarised favoured biacuplasty at 6 months, although comparators differed.
The trials directly address chronic discogenic low back pain treated with biacuplasty.
The RCTs were small (59, 63 and 44 patients) and no between-group confidence intervals are reported here.
Only three dated RCTs are summarised, so small-study and publication bias remain possible.

clinical_significance: The review does not report an MCID for these outcomes, so the effect is judged against the reported absolute changes only.
The sham-controlled pain and disability differences look clinically worthwhile, but the exact CI is not reported here.
No NNT can be derived from the summary for the pain score changes.
Meaningful benefit is plausible, but the size and durability of benefit remain uncertain.
comparator_fairness: Sham control is a credible comparator for expectation effects.
The conservative-management comparator is less equivalent for contact time and procedural expectation.
The review notes crossover in follow-up studies, which weakens later comparisons.
alternative_explanations: Natural history could contribute, especially in uncontrolled follow-up.
Expectation and procedural placebo effects could help explain some of the benefit.
Attrition and crossover may inflate apparent durability.
Baseline differences in some studies could have affected estimates.
spin: The review is broadly consistent with its primary message.
It does not overclaim cure, but the positive tone is stronger than the limited evidence base justifies.
fit_with_evidence: Fits the review’s own Table 2, which rates biacuplasty as moderate evidence and suggests use only in selected centres.
Consistent with the playbook position that this is a refractory-case option rather than routine care.
external_validity: ✓ Refractory chronic cases are relevant to sports-physio referral pathways
✗ Trial populations were small and selective
✗ One RCT excluded obesity and smoking, limiting transferability
would_change_my_mind: A larger sham-controlled RCT with longer follow-up and full safety reporting.
A high-quality systematic review showing no durable advantage over control.
Clear evidence that the procedural benefit is no better than expectation plus usual care.

study.patient_explanation: This treatment may help some people with long-lasting disc-related low back pain, but the evidence is still limited and the long-term safety and benefit are not fully known.
open_questions: How durable is the benefit beyond 6 months?
Which patients are most likely to respond?
What are the true complication rates?
key_findings: Biacuplasty has the best trial signal in this review.
The main gains are in pain and disability at about 6 months.
Evidence is still limited to a few small studies.
